title: Amortized Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions
claim: Centroid-based routing picks the wrong partition for outlier keys; learned support functions and predicted keys recover the true best match.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, vertical dividers, shared query marker x
description: Three side-by-side 2-D toy panels separated by thin vertical lines, each with a red square query x at the top right. Left: three colored ellipses (yellow C1, blue C2, cyan C3) hold dots and black pentagon centroids. A dashed arrow from x points to the nearest centroid cluster C1. The true best key y*(x), a red-ringed outlier, sits at the top of the stretched cyan cluster C3, so routing is wrong. Middle: each cluster appears as nested translucent polygon contours labeled f1, f2, f3, which represent support functions. A dashed arrow from x points into f3, the correct cluster. Right: gray dots with no clusters. A red arrow from x ends at a checkered red square, the prediction ŷ(x), which lies next to the red circle of the true key. The eye goes first to the red x in each panel.
caption: Two complementary uses of amortized MIPS. (left) the default coarse step in inverted-file indices scores the query x against each cluster centroid ci to decide the highest-scoring cell. Here the nearest centroid would be routed to the top-left cluster, but the true top key is an outlier near the top of the vertically-stretched rightmost cluster, so centroid routing picks the wrong cell. (middle) SupportNet learns one support function fi per cluster. Each support function is nonlinear, and quantifies, for any point x, the value of the highest dot-product between x and any of the points within the cluster, correctly selecting the cluster with the best attainable match even when its centroid is less aligned with x: f3(x) > f1(x) despite xT c1 > xT c3. (right) KeyNet is trained to predict a vector
abstract: Maximum inner product search (MIPS) is a crucial subroutine in machine learning, requiring the identification of a vector taken within a database (the keys) that best aligns with a given query. We propose amortized MIPS: a regression-based approach that trains neural networks to directly predict MIPS solutions, amortizing the cost of repeatedly solving MIPS for queries drawn from a known distribution over a fixed key database. Our key insight is that the MIPS value function is the \emph{support} function of the set of keys, a well-studied convex function whose gradient yields the optimal key. This motivates two complementary amortized models: SupportNet, an input-convex neural network trained to regress the support function, and KeyNet, a vector-valued network that directly regresses the optimal key. SupportNet can serve as a cluster router, steering queries toward relevant database partitions, while KeyNet can be used as a drop-in replacement for the original query, fed directly to off-the-shelf indexing pipelines. Our experiments on the BEIR benchmark show that, for document embeddings, learned \SupportNet{}s and \KeyNet{}s significantly improve IVF match rates when accounting for compute effort, whether measured in FLOPs, number of probes, or wall-clock time. Our code is available at: https://github.com/apple/ml-amips.
